summary:
MARS: The Last Green is an educational survival game prototype set at a Martian research base with an experimental greenhouse. Players take the role of an astronaut responding to a solar storm that raises outdoor radiation levels. A handheld dosimeter warns them to seek shelter, where they discover that the greenhouse has lost power.

With only three units of backup power available, players must prioritize heating and water circulation to protect the plants, leaving grow lights and Earth communications offline. The mission ends on the next sol, with a sunrise and a faint green aurora inspired by NASA’s observations of Mars.

Our project addresses the challenge by turning space science into decisions players can experience directly. Radiation awareness and limited resources become part of a short, interactive mission. This matters because protecting life beyond Earth requires understanding hazards and making difficult trade-offs. The game makes these ideas accessible while encouraging curiosity about planetary exploration.
details:
MARS: The Last Green is a first-person educational survival game prototype set at a research base on Mars. Players act as an astronaut responsible for protecting an experimental greenhouse during a solar storm. The project turns the challenges of living beyond Earth into a short mission built around observation and decision-making.

The mission begins outdoors, where a handheld dosimeter warns the player about increased radiation. The player must take shelter and investigate a power failure affecting the greenhouse. Only three units of backup power are available, so the player must prioritize heating and water circulation while leaving grow lights and Earth communications offline. The story concludes on the next sol, with a sunrise and a faint green aurora inspired by NASA’s observations of Mars.

Our current Unity prototype provides the foundation for this mission: keyboard-and-mouse movement, physical collisions, separate outdoor and indoor scenes, an inventory, animated astronaut hands, and interactive objects. The dosimeter displays both the current radiation rate and accumulated exposure. Readings change with the environment, and shelter reduces exposure. Green, yellow, and red indicators communicate the status of each reading. The greenhouse power-allocation sequence forms the next stage of the mission design.

The intended benefit is to make space science understandable through experience. Players can see how exposure accumulates and why entering shelter matters. The limited-power scenario introduces another important idea: keeping a habitat alive requires choosing which systems matter most under pressure. We aim to encourage curiosity about Mars exploration and help learners connect scientific concepts with practical consequences.

We developed the prototype on Windows using Unity 6 and C#. We used Unity’s New Input System for controls, Rigidbody physics for movement and collisions, the Universal Render Pipeline for rendering, and uGUI with TextMeshPro for interfaces. Imported FBX models provide the astronaut arms and dosimeter. Codex assisted with coding, scene automation, debugging, and testing through Unity CLI and Unity Pipeline. The prototype uses a standard computer with a keyboard and mouse.

The project’s creativity comes from combining a personal, visible warning device with a mission about protecting plant life. Players experience environmental danger through equipment they carry, then make a resource-allocation decision with a clear purpose. Our design considers scientific clarity, readable interfaces, consistent controls, and the scope of a short playable demonstration. Radiation values and warning thresholds remain simplified gameplay parameters rather than validated astronaut safety limits.
